He held her gaze for a long, tense moment. Her anger and indignation warred with a humiliating sense of her own powerlessness. He was right. She knew he was right. His logic was as unassailable as his will. She felt the fight go out of her, leaving her feeling weak and strangely young. Her eyes fell before his.

"I will see to the list," she said, her voice muffled.

She turned and walked back to the house, her head held high, but feeling the burn of a hundred eyes on her back. She had challenged him, and she had been defeated. It was a complete and utter rout.

Later that day, as she was sitting with Arthur, Ransome entered the room. He had been out on the estate for hours, and his boots were caked with mud. He carried a small, exquisite spray of wild orchids. Without a word, he placed them in a vase of water on the table beside Arthur's bed.

Arthur, who was stronger now and sitting up in a chair by the window, watched him with curious eyes. "They are fine specimens, Mr. Ransome," he said. "From the jungle edge?"

"From the gorge by the waterfall," Ransome replied. "I was inspecting the old aqueduct." He turned his attention to Ellen. "I am riding to the port to-morrow to arrange for supplies and a line of credit with the bank. Is your list ready?"

"Yes," she said, handing him a sheet of paper.

He glanced at it briefly. "Good. You will ride with me."

She looked up sharply. "But Arthur--I cannot leave him."

"I can look after myself for a day, Ellen," Arthur put in, with a flash of his old self. "Go. The air will do you good. You look like a ghost."

"Arthur is right," Ransome said. "And I require your signature on certain documents at the bank. It is necessary that you come."

He gave a short nod of satisfaction. "We will leave at sunrise." He then turned and left the room as quietly as he had entered it, leaving the startling beauty of the orchids behind him.

Ellen looked from the flowers to her brother. "He is the most exasperating man I have ever met," she said, under her breath.

Arthur smiled faintly. "Perhaps," he said. "But I think father would have liked him."

She looked at her brother, surprised by his perception. And as she considered his words, she knew with a sudden, unbidden certainty that he was right. Her father would indeed have liked him. And that, more than anything else, was the most bewildering thought of all.

"Perhaps," he acknowledged. "But you were the catalyst. And now," he continued, releasing her hand, "I have something to say, too. I came in here to say it before I saw... all this." He gestured between her and Burke. "It seems my timing is impeccable."

He looked from one to the other, his expression serious now. "Last night, fighting that fire, I felt... alive again. For the first time in years. I wasn't a patient, or a burden. I was just a man, doing a man's work. And I knew then what I had to do."

He paused, taking a breath. "I'm leaving," he said.

Sylvia's heart gave a lurch of the old, familiar anxiety. "Leaving? But Guy, where will you go? You're not strong enough yet!"

"That's where you're wrong, Sylvia," he said gently. "I am strong enough. Burke, you know it, don't you?"

Burke nodded slowly, his eyes fixed on Guy's face. "Yes," he said. "I know it."

"I'm going to find my own way," Guy went on, his voice gaining confidence. "I've been thinking about it all day, while we were checking the fences. There's a man I know, up in Rhodesia, who is starting a new tobacco plantation. He needs men who aren't afraid of hard work. I'm going to write to him. I'm going to stand on my own two feet again. It's the only way."

The finality in his tone was unmistakable. This was not the desperate flight of a broken man, but the considered decision of one who had found himself. The devil had indeed gone out of him, and he had come back, whole and determined.

"You will always have a home here, Guy," Burke said, his voice rough with emotion.

"I know," Guy replied, and he looked at Burke with profound gratitude. "And knowing that is what gives me the strength to leave it. I can't stay here, living on your charity, being a constant reminder of... of the past. You two need to build your future. And I need to build mine."

He looked at Sylvia, and his eyes were kind. "Don't worry about me," he said, echoing the words he had spoken what seemed a lifetime ago. "I'm being good, as you see."

A silence fell upon the room, a silence not of strain, but of deep and resonant understanding. The final page of that difficult chapter had been turned, gently but decisively. Guy was no longer their shared responsibility; he was his own man, with his own path to tread.

In the days that followed, a new and peaceful rhythm established itself on the farm. The work was hard; the fifty acres of lost grazing meant that cattle had to be moved, and plans for the coming season redrawn. But it was work undertaken with a shared purpose, with a lightness of heart that made every task easier. Burke was no longer a solitary, grim figure, directing operations from a distance. He worked alongside his men, and at his side, more often than not, was Guy. The two of them, who had been separated by a chasm of resentment and misunderstanding, were now united in the common goal of healing the land.

Guy wrote his letter to Rhodesia and received a swift and affirmative reply. His friend was eager to have him. A date was set for his departure in a month's time. He threw himself into the farm work with a feverish energy, as if to prove to himself, and to them, that he was capable. He and Burke spent long days in the saddle, surveying the damage, planning new fire-breaks, their talk easy and practical. The ghost of Kieff, and of the dark times, seemed to have been banished for good.

Sylvia, meanwhile, found her own role subtly changing. She was no longer just the housekeeper, nor the anxious nurse. She was the mistress of the farm, the centre around which its life now revolved. She discussed plans with Burke over the dinner table, her opinions sought and valued. She managed the household with a new and quiet confidence, her anxieties replaced by a deep, abiding sense of peace.

Her time with Burke was precious. They did not speak often of their love; there was no need. It was present in every shared glance across the room, in the way his hand would find hers as they sat on the stoep in the evenings, watching the stars appear in the vast African sky. It was in the way he would seek her out at the end of a long day, his tired face lighting up when he saw her.

One afternoon, about a week before Guy was due to leave, Burke came to find her in the small vegetable garden she had started near the house.

"I am riding over to the Merstons'," he said, leaning on the fence. "They sent a boy over with a message. It seems the news has travelled."

She looked up, shading her eyes from the sun. "What news?"

"Our news," he said, a smile playing on his lips. "Mrs. Merston has sent her formal congratulations and an invitation to dinner. An engagement dinner, I believe she called it."

Sylvia felt a flush of colour rise in her cheeks. The world outside the farm had seemed so distant. "Oh," she said. "That's... very kind of her."

"I think it is a summons," he said, his eyes twinkling. "She wants to inspect you at close quarters. Will you ride over with me?"

"Now?" she asked, looking down at her earth-stained hands.

"No. Later. After tea," he said. It was the same request he had made before, the one she had refused because of Guy. Now, there was no reason to refuse.

"Yes, of course I will," she said.

His gaze softened. "Good," he said simply. He paused for a moment, watching her. "You look happy, Sylvia."

"I am," she said, her heart swelling. "I have never been so happy in my life."

He reached over the fence and tilted her chin up with his forefinger. "I'm going to spend the rest of my life making sure you stay that way," he said, and then he was gone, striding towards the stables, leaving her in a glow of quiet bliss.

The dinner at the Merstons' was an ordeal, but one she passed through with a surprising degree of composure. Mrs. Merston, a large, formidable woman with a booming voice, did indeed inspect her from head to foot, but there was a genuine kindness beneath her brusque exterior.

"So, you're the girl who's finally tamed our Burke," she announced to the table at large. "We'd all but given up on him. Thought he'd turn into a crabby old bachelor out there on that farm of his. It took a veld fire and a pretty face to bring him to his senses, eh?"

Burke, to Sylvia's surprise, took the teasing in good part. "It took a great deal more than that, Alice," he said quietly, his eyes meeting Sylvia's across the table. "It took a woman with more courage than any man I know."

Mrs. Merston had looked from him to Sylvia, her sharp eyes softening. "Well," she had said, in a gentler tone. "He's a good man, my dear. One of the best. You look after him."

"I will," Sylvia had promised, and it had felt like a vow.

The ride home under a full moon was magical. The air was cool and sweet, and the veld, silvered by the moonlight, seemed to stretch to infinity. For a long while they rode in a comfortable silence, their horses treading softly on the sandy track.

"You survived," Burke said at last, his voice full of gentle amusement.

"I did," she laughed. "Though I'm not sure my nerves have."

"Alice means well. She has a heart of gold, buried under about six layers of granite." He reined in his horse, and she stopped beside him. The homestead was a dark shape in the distance, a single light glowing in the window.

"Our home," he said softly. He reached out and took her hand, his gloved fingers closing over hers. "Sylvia, I don't want to wait."

"Wait?" she repeated, her heart beginning to beat a little faster.

"To be married. I want to marry you as soon as it can be arranged. Before Guy leaves. I want him to be there. Will you?"

"Yes," she whispered, her throat tight with emotion. "Oh, Burke, yes. As soon as you like."

"Then I will ride into Brennerstadt tomorrow and see the magistrate," he said decisively. "We can be married right here. On the stoep. If you would like that."

"I would like that more than anything in the world," she said.

He leaned across from his saddle and kissed her, a long, sweet kiss under the African moon. "Next week, then," he said against her lips. "Next week, you will be Mrs. Burke."

The morning of Guy's departure was bright and clear. His few belongings were packed, the cart was ready. The whole farm seemed to have turned out to say goodbye. Joe, the house-boy, stood beaming, his smile wider than ever, and the other farm hands gathered in a respectful, silent group.

Guy shook hands with each of them, and then he turned to Burke. The two men stood for a moment, looking at each other.

"Take care of yourself," Burke said, his voice gruff.

"I will. And you... you do the same. And look after her." Guy's eyes flickered towards Sylvia.

"Always," Burke said.

Guy came to her last. He took both her hands in his. "Goodbye, Sylvia," he said. "And thank you. For everything."

"Goodbye, Guy. Godspeed," she said, her eyes filling with tears. They were not tears of sorrow for his leaving, but of pride for the man he had become.

He squeezed her hands, then turned and climbed into the cart without a backward glance. He was not running away from his past; he was striding towards his future. They watched until the cart was a small speck in the distance, and then Burke put his arm around her shoulders.

"He'll be all right," he said, as much to himself as to her.

"Yes," she said, leaning her head against his shoulder. "He has come back."

Two days later, they were married. The magistrate came out from Brennerstadt, a stout, balding man with a kind face. The Merstons came, as did a few other neighbouring farmers. Joe and the other servants stood at a respectful distance, their faces shining.

Sylvia wore a simple white dress she had painstakingly altered from one of her few good frocks. In her hands, she carried not a bouquet of hothouse flowers, but a small posy of wild veld lilies, their petals white and perfect.

They stood on the stoep where he had first seen her, the place where their life together had truly begun. Burke's hand was firm and steady as he took hers. He wore a sober suit, but he looked less like a grim farmer and more like a king surveying his domain. His domain, and hers.

The magistrate's words were simple, the vows ancient and profound. When Burke slid the plain gold band onto her finger, his eyes never left her face. They held a look of such deep, abiding love that her heart felt it might burst.

"I now pronounce you man and wife," the magistrate declared.

Burke did not wait for the invitation. He drew his wife into his arms and kissed her, there in front of everyone, a kiss that sealed their past, blessed their present, and promised a future as wide and as full of light as the African sky above them.

Later, when their guests had departed and a deep, peaceful twilight was settling over the land, they stood in that same spot, his arm around her. The fire-scarred patch on the horizon was already showing the faintest haze of new green. The land was healing. They were whole.

"Mrs. Burke," he said softly, trying out the sound of it. "How does it feel?"

She turned in the circle of his arm and looked up at his beloved face. The last of the sun's rays caught in his hair, turning it to bronze. All the harsh lines of strain and loneliness were gone, smoothed away by happiness.

"It feels," she said, her voice full of a quiet, unshakable certainty, "like I have come home."
